newsitem.title: GERMANY: Gorbachev says Bonn settling scores with E Germany.
newsitem.headline: Gorbachev says Bonn settling scores with E Germany.

text.p: Former Soviet president Mikhail Gorbachev has accused Bonn of settling scores with East Germany's former communist leaders by breaking a promise not to try them for actions which were legal in East Germany.

Gorbachev made his comments in a statement in support of East Berlin's last hardline leader Egon Krenz and three other former rulers, on trial for the policy of shooting refugees as they tried to escape west across East Germany's fortified border.

"At German unification in 1989-90 it was agreed with West Germany's leaders both at a confidential and an official level that disputed issues, including the legitimacy of actions which did not infringe East German law, could not be resolved through the prosecution of former political opponents," Gorbachev wrote in a two-page letter read by the defence on Monday.

As Soviet leader in 1990, Gorbachev had to approve the terms of the "Two-plus-Four" agreement in which the four World War Two victor powers gave full sovereignty back to East and West Germany upon unification.
He and his advisers agreed many awkward issues in personal talks with German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, then-foreign minister Hans-Dietrich Genscher and their aides.

Gorbachev said he discerned "a visible attempt to use the justice system to settle scores with East Germany's former officials" and said certain people were conducting a "witchhunt" to distract from Germany's other problems.
Krenz's lawyer Dieter Wissgott requested that Kohl be summoned to testify. If what Gorbachev said was true, the trial woud have to be abandoned, he said.

United Germany's justice system has struggled to bring communist leaders to account for the acts of a totalitarian state which was not regulated by law. Many are now dead, like long-time leader Erich Honecker, or too ill to face trial.

The decision to bring charges over the border killings, which appeared punishable under East German law, seemed to be vindicated last month when the supreme court rejected an appeal from three ex-Politburo members convicted on similar charges.
The Constitutional Court said East Germany's leaders could be held legally responsible for the killings and sent the men, including former defence minister Heinz Kessler, to jail.

Gorbachev, whom Kohl has often thanked for allowing German unification to go ahead so smoothly, said it was absurd to try to convict the very officials with whom West German leaders for years maintained intensive relations.
"Is it dignified to make one's former partners into scapegoats?" he asked.
